title: Secretary
full_review:
A young woman who compulsively mutilates herself finds release when she becomes the sexual slave of a sadistic boss in the perverted black comedy "Secretary" (Lions Gate).

Just out of an institution, troubled mid-20s Lee (Maggie Gyllenhaal) returns home to her alcoholic father (Stephen McHattie) and overprotective mom (Lesley Ann Warren), and quickly reverts to cutting her arms and legs. She takes a positive step, however, when she finishes typing classes and lands a secretarial job with the very strange and intimidating E. Edward Grey (James Spader), whose gloomy, cavernous offices look like a cross between a funeral parlor and the inside of an Egyptian burial chamber.

Lee fetches his coffee and actually welcomes his sneering insults and nosy personal questions. But when Grey becomes incensed one day by the typos she's made, he subjects her to a humiliating spanking. Lee is thrilled and feels liberated. The more demeaning he is to her the happier she is. Soon she is crawling on all fours to deliver correspondence to him and wearing a bar-chain across her shoulders with her arms cuffed to it.

When Grey decides he's had enough and fires her, Lee is crestfallen, to the point of agreeing to marry the wimpish Peter (Jeremy Davies). But her need for punishment reasserts itself, prompting Lee to flee Peter and go on a starvation strike in Grey's office in hopes of shaming him back into a master-slave relationship.

Director Steven Shainberg presents a positive portrait of sadomasochism as wonderfully freeing and fulfilling even as Lee embraces every degradation, only wanting more. We see that her home life is frustrating as she cowers during fights between her mother and abusive father. Her lack of self-esteem drives her to slicing into her own skin, but the script leaves the Grey character's sexual obsessions a creepy mystery. In fact, virtually everyone in the script is dysfunctional; besides Grey, Lee and her parents, fiance Peter had a nervous breakdown and his parents are unbearably pushy and smothering.

The one-note focus on aberrant sexuality becomes as repellant as the suggestion that Lee is a heroine for insisting on reveling in such sadomasochism. She becomes intensely proud of all her scars, the living proof of her years of willing self-mutilation.

Sadly, there is little true insight in this film which prefers to simply attack the values of more traditional viewers and tack on a smugly happy ending.

Due to several scenes of sadomasochistic acts, masturbation, sexual encounters, brief full nudity, fleeting violence and a few instances of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
